### Question 1

Screening is like the metal detector at an airport door: everyone walks through, including people who feel completely fine and have nothing in their pockets. When it beeps, that does not mean 'you have a weapon' — it means 'let us look closer.' That is the whole idea of screening: it is aimed at people who feel fine, and its answer is a maybe, not a verdict. Going to a clinician because you already feel sick is a different activity entirely.

### Question 2

Sensitivity is how good your net is at catching the fish that are actually in the pond. If there are 100 fish and your net brings up 90 of them, the net is 90% sensitive. Notice this says nothing about how much seaweed and how many old boots you also dragged up — that is a separate measure. Screening tests are usually built to be very sensitive, because the worst outcome at this stage is letting a real case swim right through.

### Question 3

A positive screen is a smoke alarm going off. The alarm does not mean the house is burning down; it means someone should go check the kitchen. Often it is burnt toast. Nobody sprays the whole room with a fire extinguisher before looking. That 'going to look' step is the diagnostic test, and skipping it is how people end up treated for something they never had.

### Question 4

Think of the aggressiveness setting on a spam filter. Crank it up and almost no junk reaches your inbox — but a friend's invitation lands in the spam folder too. Dial it down and every real message arrives, buried in junk. Moving a screening cutoff is exactly that dial: loosen it and you catch nearly every real case, while also flagging plenty of people who are perfectly fine. One dial, two consequences that always move in opposite directions.

### Question 5

Picture the same trained detection dog working a border crossing where smuggling is common, then working a school hallway where it essentially never happens. The dog's nose is identical in both places. At the crossing, most alerts are the real thing; in the hallway, nearly every alert turns out to be somebody's sandwich. Nothing about the dog changed — what changed is how much of the real thing was there to find. How common a condition is decides how much a positive result actually means.

### Question 6

Think of two runners who cross the finish line at the exact same second, but one of them started her stopwatch two miles earlier. Her recorded 'time on the course' looks much longer, even though she did not finish one moment later. Screening starts the stopwatch earlier by finding disease before symptoms, so 'years survived after diagnosis' stretches out even when the person dies on the very same day they would have anyway. That artificial stretch has a name: lead time.

### Question 7

Screening pays off only when two things are true at the same time: the problem is already present but silent, and you can actually do something about it during that silent window. It is like checking your car's oil — low oil gives no warning sound, and topping it up genuinely prevents engine damage. Looking for something you cannot detect before symptoms, or cannot change even after you find it, just delivers the worry sooner without changing what happens.

### Question 8

Universal screening is handing an umbrella to everyone in the city. Targeted screening is handing them out only on the side of the street where it is actually raining. CT scans deliver radiation and can set off a chain of follow-up scans and lung biopsies, so we aim them at the group whose chance of having cancer is high enough that what we catch outweighs what we cause. Same test either way — who gets offered it is the entire point.

### Question 9

Treat the grades as four different pieces of advice, not a report card where D just means 'bad grade.' A and B mean the evidence says do this. C means it depends on the individual person. D means the evidence says this does more harm than good, so steer away. And an I statement means we genuinely do not know yet. The trap is reading D as 'unproven' — it is not; D means someone looked and found the harms winning.

### Question 10

Imagine a home inspection turning up a hairline crack in the foundation. The crack is genuinely there, so this is not a false alarm. But it was never going to widen enough to matter for the life of that house. Once it is written into the report, though, the owner pays to have the foundation redone, with all the mess and expense that involves. Screening does the same thing with real but harmless disease: a true finding whose only real consequence is the treatment it sets in motion.

### Question 11

If you judge screening by 'how long people live after we find it,' you are measuring with a ruler that screening itself bends. It starts the clock early, it disproportionately catches the slow gentle cases, and it counts findings that were never dangerous as successes. So instead, count how many people in a large group actually die of the disease over the same stretch of years. Nobody's date of death shifts merely because of when someone looked, so that number cannot be fooled by any of the three tricks.

### Question 12

Three different kinds of rules get tangled together here. First, a panel of experts reads the studies and says what actually works — that is a recommendation, and it persuades rather than compels. Second, Congress passed a law saying insurers must cover the top-rated ones without charging you at the counter — that is a coverage requirement. Third, your state legislature passed its own law requiring every newborn's heel to be pricked before discharge. Knowing which layer you are standing on tells you what is strongly advised versus what is legally required.
